item.title: The Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis: Detection, Attribution, and Network-Mediated Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2611.09208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose the Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis (NAMH), a novel extension of the adaptive markets framework that conceptualizes market efficiency as a network-dependent equilibrium emerging from long-memory predictability and cross-market information transmission. Using G20 equity indices and five commodity futures over 2001-2026, we identify Japan as the central information hub, while the United States primarily acts as an information broadcaster. Contrary to conventional expectations, systemic crises do not exhibit higher network spectral radii, challenging the assumption that crisis-related fragility necessarily manifests through increased network amplification. Instead, crisis-related spectral contributions are dominated by Australia and the United States. Importantly, variance-decomposition connectedness is more closely associated with network modularity than with spectral radius, with crisis-period increases driven primarily by cross-cluster spillovers. Notably, efficiency-based market groupings explain network connectedness only marginally compared with geography and asset class, while the middle efficiency tier consistently exhibits the greatest idiosyncratic behaviour.
item.dc:creator: Hitesh Kumar Sahu, Avishek Bhandari, Ipsita Parida

item.title: Sanctions, Evasion, and Deterrence: Evidence from Speeding Enforcement
item.description: arXiv:2611.09337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design of sanctions plays a central role in shaping reoffending behavior. We study the effects of fixed monetary fines and accumulating penalty points on speeding recidivism and liability transfer. Exploiting a large increase in sanctions in Queensland, Australia, we estimate the causal effects of these sanctions on subsequent offending and nomination of other drivers. Higher demerit points increase fine renomination, consistent with strategic blame shifting. Estimated reductions in reoffending are small among offenders facing higher fines alone. Reoffending falls by a substantial 4.6 percentage points when higher fines are accompanied by additional penalty points.
item.dc:creator: Romain Gauriot, Maria Wisniewska

item.title: Further Education During Unemployment
item.description: arXiv:2312.17123v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evidence on the effectiveness of retraining unemployed U.S. workers primarily comes from evaluations of training programs, a narrow avenue for skill acquisition. We use administrative records from Ohio to estimate the effects of retraining, broadly defined as postsecondary enrollment, via matching. Our simple method bridges two strands of the dynamic treatment effect literature that differ in whether the counterfactual allows later treatment or rules it out throughout the treatment window. Enrollees experience earnings gains of six percent three to four years after enrolling, following depressed earnings during the first two years. The gains are driven by industry-switchers, particularly to healthcare.
item.dc:creator: Pauline Leung, Zhuan Pei

item.title: Urban Reconstruction and Population Redistribution: Evidence from Tokyo after the Great Kanto Earthquake
item.description: arXiv:2607.02978v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study examines the impact of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake on population distribution within Tokyo City. Using newly digitized census statistics and variation in fire damage across areas, I show that land readjustment under the reconstruction project reduced residential land in the burned area, and rents rose throughout the city, particularly in the burned area. Although residential floor area recovered through the construction of multi-story dwellings, the number of households in the burned area remained below its pre-earthquake level, whereas the population had returned to roughly its pre-earthquake level by 1935. The pre-earthquake zoning system had little effect, suggesting that post-disaster population distribution was shaped by market-based price adjustments rather than regulation. The population in the burned area thus reflected the net effect of two opposing forces: fewer households due to the loss of residential land, partly offset by more households per dwelling through lodging, and larger households through the inclusion of non-kin members, such as servants and employees.
